accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS ELA RL.3.5 (refer to parts of stories, dramas and poems using chapter, scene and stanza; describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections) and RL.4.5 (structural elements of poems and drama, including stage directions), and the National Curriculum for England Years 3 and 4 reading. Definitions of stanza, act, scene and verse checked in the Poetry Foundation glossary; the note that verse can mean poetry in general avoids a wrong simplification.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report for this standard: counting lines instead of stanzas (the count step offers the line total and names it), calling every part a chapter (poem and play pages refuse 'Chapter'), thinking a scene is bigger than an act (the size-order step refuses it), and treating chapters or stanzas as stand-alone (the ordering and building steps reward back-pointing clues).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagparts draws real page layouts (a poem with a gap, a novel heading, a script with colons and bracketed directions, an act listing its scenes), numbers stanza blocks as they are tapped, nests parts by size and orders chapters by back-reference. No other flag lab works on text structure; it passed the 6-token shingle gate against every lab, including flagtexts and flagstage.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners see the line total next to the stanza blocks and must pick the group count, build each nesting stack from the biggest part down, and only get the chapter order right by following 'Still holding the key' and 'the gate' back to their source. The final step asks how stanzas 2 and 3 build, so the RL.3.5 'builds on earlier sections' clause is practised, not just told.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: a group of lines is a paragraph (the poem page calls it a stanza), 9 lines in 3 groups means 9 stanzas (the counter refuses 9), a scene holds acts (the size order refuses scene first), and chapters stand alone (the ordering only works by following clues back).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten distinct tags: 'scene' and 'same' for act-scene size, 'lines' and 'add' for counting, 'poem' and 'play' for which text has chapters, 'first' and 'alone' for back-references, and 'chap' and 'scn' for the wrong term for a group of lines. Each message names the slip and the right reasoning.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: learn/readability.py gives kid text FK 2.7 and adult text FK 7.5 (limits 6.5 and 9.5). Kid text uses short sentences and a running example (Ama and the key); adult text names the precise terms prose, play script, act, scene, cast list, dialogue, stage directions, stanza, line and verse.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matched; explanation overlap with Different Types of Texts, Understanding drama and performance and every other lesson stays under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph covers one text type or the building idea; adult paragraphs give the standard, the terms, the named mistakes and the lab steps.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px and iPhone 13 in light and dark themes: the page sample fits inside its card, the four term boxes sit in one row, stanza blocks are full-width tap targets, chapter cards wrap to two lines, and the sea poem's three stanzas fit above the question. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. Every canvas tap has a button: the four terms, each stanza block and each count, each part (in shuffled order so the buttons do not give the answer), each chapter (full text in its aria-label) and each answer. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action.

sources: Common Core State Standards for ELA: RL.3.5 and RL.4.5
DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England, English programmes of study: Years 3 and 4 reading comprehension
Poetry Foundation glossary of poetic terms: stanza, verse, line
